title: Understanding drug use in Waterloo Region
subtitle: Committee also received housing and homelessness plan and infectious disease reports, and asked for an updated tracking list.
overview: The Community and Health Services Committee heard a public health presentation, Understanding Drug Use in Waterloo Region. Staff and a community drug strategy representative described local drug use data, contributing factors such as housing instability and mental illness, and the programs run by the Region and its partners. The report was received for information, so it did not involve a recommendation to Council.

Through the consent agenda, the committee received the 2023 annual report on the 10-Year Housing and Homelessness Plan and the 2023 infectious disease highlights {{vote:m1}}. No items were pulled for discussion.

Councillors pressed staff on whether current strategies are working, how drug use is measured, and where gaps in treatment remain. Staff said the drug supply has become more toxic and that more treatment capacity and provincial funding are needed. The committee also asked that the Council and Committee Tracking List be updated with current completion dates.
The committee then moved to a closed session on a proposed land purchase and a personal matter about an identifiable individual. The next meeting is August 13, 2024.

decisions.detail: The committee received for information, and approved, the 2023 Housing and Homelessness Plan annual report and the 2023 Infectious Disease Highlights report.

debate: Several councillors questioned whether current strategies will reduce deaths and drug use. Staff said the rise in the number of people counted is partly because the needle syringe program now serves more people, so comparisons with earlier years are not like for like.

A councillor asked how the estimate of people using drugs was reached and what it covers. Staff said it comes from needle syringe program clients and is likely an underestimate. Another councillor asked how people who become dependent after medical treatment find help; staff said people mostly seek it themselves or through a primary care provider.

Staff said drugs and drug combinations have become more toxic across Ontario, which is driving more overdoses and alerts. Safe supply was described as one option still being assessed by Health Canada and needing more research before wider use.

The Regional Chair asked for objective measures of effectiveness. Staff pointed to program indicators and reporting from the consumption and treatment services site, and said numbers would likely be higher without current services.

A delegate from the drug strategy said treatment and recovery beds are full, so clients are often driven to other cities. Recovery homes have only recently received regional funding and have no provincial funding. The delegate also noted that provincial rules do not allow inhalation services at consumption sites, while urgent public health need sites can be more flexible. A councillor asked for more information on how those sites operate and for reporting on all drug deaths, not only opioid deaths; staff said they rely on Office of the Chief Coroner data.
